text:
Default `[]` is built once, when Python defines `add`. Every call that omits `items` reuses that same list.

`add(1)` appends `1`. `add(2)` appends `2` onto the same list, so the result is `[1, 2]`.

Fix: default `None`, then make a new list inside the function.

```python
def add(x, items=None):
    if items is None:
        items = []
    items.append(x)
    return items
```

`add(1)` returns `[1]`. `add(2)` returns `[2]`. Pass your own list when you want to keep appending: `add(3, items)`.
thought:
This is a classic Python gotcha involving mutable default arguments.

The default list is created once at function definition time and shared across all calls. Each call appends to the same underlying list object, so values accumulate across invocations.

Use `None` as the default argument and create a fresh list inside the function body. This prevents the shared mutable state.
